utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, good afternoon to you all. I would like the Registrar to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-66-R77, the Prosecutor versus Beqa Beqaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. I will now turn to the Prosecution, and remind them of the decision that has been rendered by the Trial Chamber on the 24th of February 2005 relating to protective measures. If I have understood this correctly, these protective measures had been agreed upon in the Limaj case and are applicable mutatis mutandis, pursuant to Rule 75(F)(i) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Have you asked for any other protective measures or different protective measures? Mr. Beqaj, can you follow the proceedings in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher, please, would you mind assisting Mr. Beqaj. Yes. Can you hear now? Can you hear me in a language that I understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Beqaj. So I shall now turn to the Prosecution. The protective measures that have been granted to Witness B1 are -- do they apply in the same way as contained in the decision taken on the 24th of February 2005?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, David Akerson on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. And to my right is Jason Dominguez and my case manager, Sebastiaan von Hooydonk. Yes, not only does the protection measures from the Limaj trial carry over into this trial but we filed a motion confirming that as well, asking for the same protection measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These protective measures were granted by the decision which I have just mentioned. I think you can now call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, we are ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher, would you kindly drop the blinds and bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before providing your evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration. The usher will show you the text of this solemn declaration and I would like to you read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, you may sit down. Mr. Akerson, will you be leading the evidence of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed. You have the floor. But before identifying the witness, either you hand him out a sheet of paper which contains his name, or we would have to move for two or three minutes into private session. How are you going to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that we start in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Registrar, could we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours may --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the witness has identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: How do you know Beqa Beqaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: I know him because he's a co-villager. He was and still is my co-villager even though he has changed now, the village he lives in Shtime. I knew him since I was young. My parents, my grandfathers knew him. The entire family knew him. We had good relations with his family. We worked together sometimes. So I know him as I said since a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: And what -- to the best of your knowledge, what is Beqa Beqaj's relationship to Isak Musliu?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: As to the relationship of Beqa Beqaj to Isak Musliu, I never knew anything about it before. If someone told me that they had a relationship, I wouldn't believe it. But to be frank with you, I don't know what exact relationship they have, whether they are in-laws or not. But I do know that there is a relationship, a family relationship. I cannot be precise as to what kind of relationship that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Do you know Bashkim Beqaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: No. I have never known him.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Have you ever heard the name before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: The name I've heard, when I came here, because in the past, I

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Are you aware of his relationship to Beqa Beqaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: I've heard that Bashkim is Beqa's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I know in the village of Shtime, the village is divided into neighbourhoods that are related to families.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm going to need to move into private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session, please, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to talk about the threats and intimidations that you received that led to that level of witness protection being assigned to you in November of 2003, and I'd like you to start by telling the judges about the first assassination attempt on your life in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: Yes but for this we need to move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: That's fine, could we meet into closed or private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session, Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Okay. So after the second assassination attempt and you are in close protection for eight months, which is very difficult, I know, you decide to leave. Can you tell the Court what happens at that point.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: I thought that, as the Prosecutors told me, the persons who had committed the murders and maltreated people would be arrested, even though, as I said, I didn't know how long it takes for these things to happen. But when the UNMIK police took very long to do things and conduct investigations, the most difficult thing for me was to see my kids staying home and not going to school, to stay as I am now in a hall like there and see your children unable to go to school. For me this was very difficult. And then I had a conversation, then I said, "I am willing to accept any assassination attempt but I can't stand it any more. Even if I lived for a week or two weeks, I preferred to be free." So I signed to go back to the place where I used to work, even though I was facing major difficulties, because the firm I was working for had dismissed me and for eight months they hadn't paid anything. But I still returned. To cut a long story short, I found another job. I settled down there, and kept in touch with the UNMIK police. They told me that now the situation has become very grave and it is going to be treated by the Tribunal, the Hague Tribunal. And the work with the Hague Tribunal investigators began. They asked me to give a statement from the beginning, from A to Z, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: (redacted) Are you put into any kind of protection by the police at this point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: At that time, I refused protection. I refused close protection, as they called it, but in a way, I was protected. I had always to inform them when I was sleeping, when I was working, which of the persons I was working with, things which they wanted me to tell them.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were back in that country. And now in the period that you arrive back in that country, up until November 2003 when you were officially put into ICTY witness protection, can you tell the Court the threats that you received because you were a witness. Starting with, I would like you to start with the phone calls that you personally get, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: Firstly, when I returned there with the help of the company, I found a house to bring my family. In a way, I had lost confidence even in the UNMIK police and the ICTY investigators. I had the impression they weren't doing anything for me. When the fact was I had seen a massacre, I was an eyewitness and one, two years had passed and nothing was done, then I lost completely lost trust and thought to bring my children and family and work there, even though, as I (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: On Saturday, I returned home. There were some relatives of mine there besides my family. Before I received the direct threat from someone from Kosova, when I heard about the procedures here, what was happening in the Trial Chamber, I had received threats through telephone. I had received threatening phone calls telling me to withdraw my testimony, my statement, because otherwise you will never come back to Kosova, you will never see Kosova again. They often they told me we will kill you in two weeks, in 10 days. If you don't withdraw your statement, they told me, if you don't do it publicly, you will be killed. These were all words and threats made against me via telephone. After that, a friend of mine came -- I don't know if we are in closed session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Are we still in closed session? We are in open session now? Can we go into closed session for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: At this stage, you were put into ICTY witness protection because of all of these events. And can you describe to the court what that protection involves, for you and your family.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: The protection measures were so that I could escape death, so that I could not get killed. What protection can be else for?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Let me ask the question a different way, as far as where you were living. What -- did they relocate you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: For the moment, no. Although I have completed secondary school, I don't know the circumstances in which the security forces work. However, in a very short time, I got an authorisation from the authorities to withdraw from that place where I was living and it was very difficult for me and my family. I had used to that place. I had -- I was used to work with that family, and my family as well was used to that place. But their explanation was in order for you to be safe and not to get killed, you have to move from this place. And I was forced to accept that. Everything was difficult for us but in order to survive, I had to do everything, as they told me. Therefore, I had to move from the original place where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: And what about your telephones? Were you allowed to keep your old telephone numbers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: During the first move, that happened through the phone that is we had. I had a phone, my wife had a phone. So these were the phones that were used. Although everyone who was interested in the trial proceedings followed the proceedings. I did the same. And as the trial approached, that's how tension rose. Especially three, four months before the trial began. This is what the authorities there, security there, told me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: My question to you is: As part of the witness protection programme, did you have to change the place where you were living and the phone numbers that you had, in order to protect you? And how many times was that done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: Six months prior to the commencement of the trial, I had to change my place of living, of residence, for three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: So just so we are clear, from November 2003 until about six months before trial, you had to change your residence and associated phone numbers about three times, or three times, sorry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: Three times, and this is all because of the security issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you also had at that time close protection. You were assigned law enforcement officers to protect you. And how many and where were those people in proximity to you and your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: In fact, I could not leave my apartment at all without informing the protection forces. They were at all times in civilian clothes, and my extra meetings with investigators or similar figures, I was escorted by cars. But just for a simple thing like having a coffee in a restaurant, I was escorted by three or four persons, and this was very difficult. And I wouldn't want you to misunderstand me, but even to go to a toilet was difficult because you were aware that three persons were waiting there and keeping eye on you while you're there. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: (redacted) I had to work for them. But the Tribunal explained that this was only for my protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you here and ask a question. This witness protection, which I understand was very difficult, very difficult on you and your family, that involved you changing your residence and your phone numbers and having these close protection officers with you at all times, that was the situation at the time that you first get contact from Beqa Beqaj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: This was the situation before, during and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: So my question to you is: With this -- with this level of protection that was in place, if someone -- who could contact you? That's the question I should ask. Who could contact you with that kind of protection in place? Who had the ability to contact you?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Now, you're referring to direct contact, I presume. How many people had your phone number that were able to call you? Because your phone numbers were changing as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B1
utterances.text: This is how it was at the time as for the phone number. Are we in closed session or open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Can we move into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Akerson, you may proceed, but I think we are now in open session, aren't we, Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, I'm sorry, are we now in private session or -- and we are moving into open session, aren't we, Mr. Akerson? Or do we stay in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this needs to be in private session because we are referring to a relative's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's stay in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, 28 April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.37 p.m.,
